overview.intro:
Chapter 68 covers worked stone — granite, marble, travertine, quartzite, slate — and the man-made materials around it: engineered quartz and concrete articles, gypsum board, mineral wool, asphalt roofing, fiber-cement, grinding wheels and sandpaper, friction material, asbestos articles, mica and carbon fiber. **Base rates are low**: 42 of the 97 tariff lines are dutiable, at 1.9% to 9% — granite 3.7%, marble slabs 2.5%, quartzite and other stone 6.5%, mineral wool 3.9% — and engineered quartz slabs are Free.

The U.S. imported **$9.57B** of these goods in 2025: $3.09B of worked stone (heading 6802) and $2.46B of concrete and artificial-stone articles, engineered quartz included. **Mexico** ($1.04B) and **Canada** ($1.03B) led, ahead of Brazil, India, Italy and China. The extra duty decides the price: since **August 15, 2026** engineered quartz pays a **Section 201 safeguard** of +25% in quota or +50% over quota (Canada, Mexico, Brazil, Israel, Korea and other listed countries excluded), on top of a **Section 301 tariff** on 60 economies (+10% India, +12.5% Turkey, Vietnam and Thailand, 10% in total for the EU). China pays +37.5% on every line, and Chinese, Indian and Turkish quartz also carries **antidumping and countervailing duties**. Brazilian granite pays 41.2%, but **Brazilian quartzite is exempt** from the 25% Brazil duty (19% in total). Canadian gypsum board and 6810.99 articles owe a **50% Section 338 duty even under USMCA**, and EPA bans the import of chrysotile asbestos brakes and gaskets.

productGroups.label: Setts, curbstones & flagstones of natural stone
productGroups.blurb: Setts (paving cubes), curbstones and flagstones of natural stone other than slate pay 2.8%.

productGroups.label: Worked stone: granite, marble, travertine, quartzite & other monumental or building stone
productGroups.blurb: The rate follows the stone and how far it is worked. Granite slabs, countertops and monuments pay 3.7%; marble slabs 2.5%, other worked marble 4.9% (simply cut or sawn 1.9%); travertine 3.7%–4.2%; limestone and other calcareous stone 4.9%; quartzite, sandstone, slate-free mosaics and "other stone" 6%–6.5%; small tiles and cubes under 7 cm and colored granules 4.8%. Rough blocks are in Chapter 25.

productGroups.label: Worked slate & slate articles (incl. roofing slate)
productGroups.blurb: Roofing slate pays 3.3%; other worked slate — tiles, flooring, slabs — is Free.

productGroups.label: Millstones, grindstones & grinding wheels (incl. diamond and resin-bonded)
productGroups.blurb: Most grinding articles are Free: millstones, diamond wheels and saw-blade segments, vitrified abrasive wheels, natural sharpening stones. Wheels bonded with synthetic resin pay 5¢/kg + 2%. Diamond saw-blade segments from China fall under a Commerce antidumping order.

productGroups.label: Coated abrasives: sandpaper, abrasive cloth, belts & discs
productGroups.blurb: Sandpaper, emery cloth, sanding belts, discs and sponges — abrasive on a backing of cloth, paper or other material — are all Free.

productGroups.label: Mineral wool (rock & slag wool), vermiculite & expanded clays
productGroups.blurb: Rock wool and slag wool insulation — batts, boards, pipe coverings and acoustical pads — pays 3.9%; exfoliated vermiculite, expanded clays, foamed slag, calcium silicate and other heat- or sound-insulating mineral mixtures are Free.

productGroups.label: Asphalt articles: roofing rolls, shingles & siding
productGroups.blurb: Asphalt roofing in rolls is Free; asphalt shingles, siding and other asphalt articles pay 2.7%.

productGroups.label: Wood-wool, straw & fiber panels bonded with cement or plaster
productGroups.blurb: Panels, boards, tiles and blocks of wood wool, shavings, straw or other vegetable fiber bonded with cement, plaster or another mineral binder are Free.

productGroups.label: Plaster articles: gypsum board (drywall), plaster panels & tiles
productGroups.blurb: Gypsum board (drywall, plasterboard) faced with paper is Free; other plaster boards and tiles pay 3%; ornamented plaster articles and molds are Free. Gypsum board from Canada pays the 50% Section 338 duty, even under USMCA.

productGroups.label: Cement, concrete & artificial stone: engineered quartz slabs, tiles, blocks & precast
productGroups.blurb: Engineered quartz slabs (6810.99.00.20/.40) are Free in the base column but carry the 2026 safeguard tariff (+25% in quota, +50% over quota) from most countries, and antidumping and countervailing duties from China, India and Turkey. Agglomerated-stone floor tiles pay 4.9%, other cement or concrete tiles 9%, concrete blocks and bricks 3.2%, other articles 3.9%; precast structural parts are Free.

productGroups.label: Fiber-cement (asbestos-cement and cellulose fiber-cement) sheets, panels & pipes
productGroups.blurb: Fiber-cement sheets, corrugated roofing, panels, pipes and siding are Free. Articles that contain asbestos (6811.40) are Free in the tariff but need EPA notice under the asbestos significant new use rule before they are imported.

productGroups.label: Asbestos fibers & articles: gaskets, jointing, paper, clothing
productGroups.blurb: Asbestos footwear pays 8.3%; other asbestos clothing, paper, millboard, compressed-fiber jointing and gaskets are Free. EPA bans the import of chrysotile asbestos for gaskets and vehicle friction products.

productGroups.label: Friction material: unmounted brake linings & pads, clutch facings
productGroups.blurb: Unmounted friction material — brake linings and pads, clutch facings, sheets and rolls — is Free, with or without asbestos. Brake pads mounted for motor vehicles are classified with vehicle parts (8708.30).

productGroups.label: Worked mica & mica articles
productGroups.blurb: Mica plates and sheets of agglomerated or reconstituted mica pay 2.7%; other worked mica 2.6%.

productGroups.label: Other mineral articles: carbon fiber, graphite, peat, magnesia & talc articles
productGroups.blurb: Carbon fibers, carbon-fiber fabric and other non-electrical carbon-fiber articles are Free, as are graphite articles, peat articles, magnesia and magnesia-carbon refractory shapes, and cut talc or soapstone. Magnesia carbon bricks from China and Mexico fall under Commerce antidumping (and, for China, countervailing) orders.

workedExamples.title: Engineered quartz slab from Vietnam (in quota)
workedExamples.body: The base rate is Free. Vietnam adds the 12.5% Section 301 duty (9903.05.84) and, because the slab is a quartz surface product under U.S. note 41 and Vietnam is not on the note 41(c) exclusion list, the safeguard tariff: +25% while the quarterly quota is open (9903.45.30), **37.5%** in total — $3,750 on a $10,000 slab shipment. Once the quarter's 3,251,606 m² quota is filled, the same slab enters under 9903.45.31 at +50%: **62.5%**. No antidumping order covers Vietnamese quartz.

workedExamples.title: Engineered quartz countertops from China
workedExamples.body: China pays +12.5% (9903.05.31) and +25% (List 3, 9903.88.03), plus the safeguard (+25% in quota or +50% over quota): **62.5% or 87.5%** before trade remedies. On top come the 2019 antidumping and countervailing duty orders on Chinese quartz surface products — set at 326.15% (China-wide cash deposit) and 45.32% (all others) when the orders were issued — so Chinese quartz is priced out of the U.S. market.

workedExamples.title: Quartzite and granite slabs from Brazil
workedExamples.body: Brazil pays the 12.5% Section 301 duty (9903.05.27) and the 25% Brazil Section 301 duty (9903.05.01) — but 6802.99.00, the line for quartzite and other stone, is on the Brazil exemption list in U.S. note 50(a)(ii), so a quartzite slab pays 6.5% + 12.5% = **19%**. A Brazilian granite slab (6802.93.00.25, 3.7%) pays all three: **41.2%**. Natural quartzite is not a quartz surface product, so no safeguard applies.

workedExamples.title: Marble slabs from Italy or Turkey
workedExamples.body: Polished marble slabs pay 2.5%. For EU goods with a base rate under 10%, the 2026 Section 301 action charges 10% in total (9903.05.39): **10%**, $1,000 on $10,000 of Carrara slabs. Turkish marble pays 2.5% + 12.5% (9903.05.79) = **15%**.

workedExamples.title: Gypsum board (drywall) from Canada
workedExamples.body: Paper-faced gypsum board is Free and USMCA-qualifying goods skip the 10% Section 301 duty (9903.05.93). But 6809.11.00 is on the Section 338 list in U.S. note 51(b)(3) (9903.03.14), and that 50% applies even when USMCA is claimed: **50%**, $5,000 on a $10,000 load. A non-qualifying load pays 60%.

tariffUpdates.h1: HTS Chapter 68: Stone, Quartz, Plaster, Cement & Abrasives — Tariff Updates

seo.title: HTS Chapter 68 Tariff Updates 2026: Quartz Safeguard, Granite & Stone Duties Since January 2025 | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: What changed for HTS Chapter 68 — granite, marble, quartzite, engineered quartz, gypsum board, abrasives, mineral wool — since January 2025: the 2026 Section 201 quartz safeguard (25%/50%), the end of the IEEPA and Section 122 duties, the Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies, China List 3, Brazil and Canada Section 338, and the quartz antidumping orders, with Federal Register citations.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule: the **2025 Basic Edition**, in force at the start of 2025, and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026). **No Chapter 68 base rate changed**: all 97 lines carry the same General, Special and Column 2 rates, from Free to 9%.

What changed sits on top of the base rate. In 2025 the IEEPA duties reached stone and building materials from every country — 15% in total for EU marble and granite and 15% for Turkey from August 7, 2025, 50% for India from August 27, 50% for most Brazilian stone (quartzite exempt), and up to 125% for China in April–May 2025 on top of the 25% List 3 duty. The IEEPA duties **ended on February 24, 2026**, and the 10% Section 122 surcharge that replaced them expired on July 23, 2026. Since **July 24, 2026** goods from 60 economies pay a **Section 301 tariff** (+10% India and the UK, +12.5% Turkey, Vietnam and Brazil, 10% in total for the EU); China still pays the **25% List 3 duty** on every Chapter 68 line, and Brazil a further 25% on everything but quartzite and other stone of 6802.99. Since **August 15, 2026** engineered quartz slabs and countertops pay a **Section 201 safeguard** — +25% in quota, +50% over quota — unless they come from Canada, Mexico, an FTA partner or a listed developing country. Since **August 22, 2026** Canadian gypsum board and 6810.99 articles pay a **50% Section 338 duty**, even under USMCA.

Trade remedies run alongside: Commerce antidumping and countervailing duty orders cover quartz surface products from **China** (2019) and **India and Turkey** (2020) — all continued after five-year reviews — diamond saw-blade segments and sol-gel abrasive grains from China, and magnesia carbon bricks from China and Mexico.
tariffUpdates.scope: Measures that reach Chapter 68 from any country: the 2026 Section 201 safeguard on quartz surface products (U.S. note 41), the 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies, the Brazil Section 301 tariff and its exemption for 6802.99.00, the China Section 301 List 3 duty and its one product exclusion, the Canada Section 338 duties, Russia's rates in lieu of column 2, and the 2025–2026 IEEPA and Section 122 duties that have ended. Antidumping and countervailing duty orders are described in the change log with their Federal Register notices; their company-specific rates are set by Commerce and are not part of the rates shown. EPA's chrysotile asbestos import bans are listed for reference. For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

inEffect.measure: Section 201 safeguard on quartz surface products (tariff-rate quota)
inEffect.exemption: Applies only to quartz surface products — slabs, countertops, vanity tops, tiles and other surfaces in which silica is the largest single material by weight, bound with resin — of 6810.99.00.20 and 6810.99.00.40 (and 7020.00.60 in Chapter 70), finished or not, including QSP fabricated in a third country. It does not cover granite, marble, soapstone or quartzite. Within a quarterly quota of 3,251,606 m² (13,006,426 m² for August 15, 2026–August 14, 2027) the rate is +25% (9903.45.30); entries beyond it pay +50% (9903.45.31). The duty is cumulative with the base rate and all other duties, including antidumping and countervailing duties and the Section 301 duties. Products of the countries listed in U.S. note 41(c) — Canada and Mexico; Australia, Colombia, Costa Rica, the Dominican Republic, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Israel, Nicaragua, Panama, Peru, Singapore and South Korea; the listed developing countries (among them Brazil, Indonesia, the Philippines, Cambodia, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Egypt and South Africa); and CBERA beneficiaries — are excluded and do not count against the quota. QSP admitted to a foreign-trade zone from August 15, 2026 must be in privileged foreign status.

inEffect.exemption: Two measures. The 2026 Section 301 duty (+10%, 9903.05.29) does not apply to USMCA-qualifying goods (9903.05.93). The Section 338 duty (+50%, from August 22, 2026, 9903.03.14) applies to products of Canada of 6809.11.00 (paper-faced gypsum board) and 6810.99.00 (other articles of cement, concrete or artificial stone, including quartz slabs), and U.S. note 51(a) says it applies even when USMCA or another special rate is claimed. Civil-aircraft articles are relieved (9903.03.16). Canada is excluded from the quartz safeguard (note 41(c)(i)). The 35% IEEPA duty on non-USMCA goods (9903.01.10) ended February 24, 2026.
inEffect.whatItMeans: USMCA-qualifying Canadian drywall and quartz slabs pay 50%; non-qualifying 60%. Other USMCA-qualifying Canadian goods — mineral wool, abrasives, stone, asphalt shingles — pay nothing.

inEffect.exemption: +25% under the Brazil action from July 22, 2026 (9903.05.01) and +12.5% under the 2026 action from July 24, 2026 (9903.05.27). The Brazil exemption list (U.S. note 50(a)(ii), 9903.05.03) names 6802.99.00 — quartzite, sandstone and the other "other stone" of heading 6802 — so those four lines pay only the 12.5%. Civil-aircraft articles are relieved by 9903.05.05 and 9903.05.88. Brazil is a developing country on the note 41(c) list, so its engineered quartz pays no safeguard. The 40% IEEPA duty on Brazil (Executive Order 14323, which also exempted 6802.99.00) ended February 24, 2026.
inEffect.whatItMeans: A Brazilian quartzite slab pays 19% (6.5% + 12.5%); a granite slab or countertop 41.2% (3.7% + 37.5%); marble 39.4%–42.4%.

inEffect.exemption: Base rate + 10% (9903.05.44). No Chapter 68 line is on the general exemption list (note 52(b)) or on any country exception list in note 52(j). Engineered quartz slabs and countertops (6810.99.00.20/.40) also pay the Section 201 safeguard: +25% in quota (9903.45.30) or +50% over quota (9903.45.31) — India is not on the note 41(c) exclusion list — and the 2020 antidumping and countervailing duty orders on Indian quartz surface products, continued in December 2025. The IEEPA duties on India (25% reciprocal from August 7, 2025, plus 25% from August 27, 2025) ended in February 2026.
inEffect.whatItMeans: Indian granite slabs and countertops pay 13.7%, sandstone and other stone 16.5%, slate tiles 10%; Indian engineered quartz 35% in quota or 60% over quota, plus its company antidumping and countervailing rates.

inEffect.exemption: For EU goods whose base rate is under 10% — every Chapter 68 line — the total is 10% (9903.05.39), in place of the base rate. No Chapter 68 line is on the general exemption list (note 52(b)) or on any country exception list in note 52(j). The EU is not on the note 41(c) list, so EU engineered quartz pays the safeguard on top: 35% in quota, 60% over quota. This replaced the 15%-in-total IEEPA rate (9903.02.20), which ended February 24, 2026.
inEffect.whatItMeans: Italian marble and granite, Spanish slate and limestone, German grinding wheels and mineral wool pay 10% of value — $1,000 on $10,000 — instead of 15% in late 2025 and 1.9%–6.5% before that. Spanish or Italian engineered quartz pays 35% or 60%.

inEffect.exemption: Two Section 301 duties stack on every Chapter 68 line: +12.5% under the 2026 action (9903.05.31) and +25% under List 3 (9903.88.03), which covers all Chapter 68 subheadings. The only exclusion in force (U.S. note 20(vvv)(iii), 9903.88.69) covers brown-wave and flamed sandstone pavers of the dimensions described (6802.99.00.90), through November 9, 2026. Civil-aircraft brake linings and asbestos articles of 6812–6813 that meet general note 6 are exempt (note 52(d), 9903.05.88). Engineered quartz slabs and countertops (6810.99.00.20/.40) also pay the Section 201 safeguard: +25% in quota (9903.45.30) or +50% over quota (9903.45.31), and Chinese quartz also carries the 2019 antidumping and countervailing duties. The IEEPA duties on China (fentanyl and reciprocal) ended February 24, 2026; USTR's four-year review kept List 3 in place.
inEffect.whatItMeans: Chinese granite slabs and countertops pay 41.2% (3.7% + 37.5%), marble 39.4%–42.4%, resin-bonded grinding wheels 5¢/kg + 39.5%, sandpaper and carbon fiber 37.5%; engineered quartz 62.5%–87.5% before antidumping and countervailing duties.

inEffect.exemption: Base rate + 12.5% (9903.05.79). No Chapter 68 line is on the general exemption list (note 52(b)) or on any country exception list in note 52(j). Engineered quartz slabs and countertops (6810.99.00.20/.40) also pay the Section 201 safeguard: +25% in quota (9903.45.30) or +50% over quota (9903.45.31) — Turkey is not on the note 41(c) list — and Turkish quartz surface products carry the 2020 antidumping and countervailing duty orders, continued in December 2025. The 15% IEEPA reciprocal duty ended February 24, 2026.
inEffect.whatItMeans: Turkish marble slabs pay 15%, travertine 16.2%–16.7%, other worked marble 17.4%; Turkish engineered quartz 37.5% or 62.5% plus its antidumping and countervailing rates.

inEffect.exemption: Base rate + 12.5% (9903.05.84). No Chapter 68 line is on the general exemption list (note 52(b)) or on any country exception list in note 52(j). Engineered quartz slabs and countertops (6810.99.00.20/.40) also pay the Section 201 safeguard: +25% in quota (9903.45.30) or +50% over quota (9903.45.31) — Vietnam is not on the note 41(c) list. No antidumping order covers Vietnamese Chapter 68 goods. The 20% IEEPA reciprocal duty (9903.02.69) ended February 24, 2026.
inEffect.whatItMeans: Vietnamese engineered quartz pays 37.5% in quota or 62.5% over quota; granite 16.2%, other stone 19%.

inEffect.exemption: For Japanese goods whose base rate is under 12.5% — every Chapter 68 line — the total is 12.5% (9903.05.49). No Chapter 68 line is on the general exemption list (note 52(b)) or on any country exception list in note 52(j). Japan is not on the note 41(c) list, so its quartz surface products also pay the safeguard. The 15%-in-total IEEPA rate ended February 24, 2026.
inEffect.whatItMeans: Japanese carbon fiber, grinding wheels, mica and other Chapter 68 goods pay 12.5% of value in total.

inEffect.exemption: Base rate + 12.5% (9903.05.77). No Chapter 68 line is on the general exemption list (note 52(b)) or on any country exception list in note 52(j). Engineered quartz slabs and countertops (6810.99.00.20/.40) also pay the Section 201 safeguard: +25% in quota (9903.45.30) or +50% over quota (9903.45.31) — Thailand is not on the note 41(c) list. No antidumping order covers Thai Chapter 68 goods. The 19% IEEPA reciprocal duty (9903.02.61) ended February 24, 2026.
inEffect.whatItMeans: Thai engineered quartz — the third-largest source of heading 6810 in 2025 — pays 37.5% in quota or 62.5% over quota; Thai granite 16.2%.

inEffect.exemption: For Korean goods whose base rate is under 12.5% — every Chapter 68 line — the total is 12.5% (9903.05.71). No Chapter 68 line is on the general exemption list (note 52(b)) or on any country exception list in note 52(j). Korea is on the note 41(c)(ii) list, so Korean quartz surface products pay no safeguard. The 15%-in-total IEEPA rate ended February 24, 2026.
inEffect.whatItMeans: Korean grinding wheels, coated abrasives, carbon fiber and engineered quartz pay 12.5% of value in total.

inEffect.measure: Section 301 (2026, 60 economies) + Russia (rates in lieu of column 2)
inEffect.exemption: Russia pays column 2 rates (general note 3(b)) — 13% to 60% on stone, 20%–45% on most other lines — plus +12.5% (9903.05.66). Seventeen Chapter 68 subheadings — marble slabs, slate, millstones and diamond tools, some abrasive articles, mineral wool and vermiculite, asphalt rolls, fiber-cement sheets and 6810.99 articles including quartz slabs — pay 35% under 9903.90.08 in place of their column 2 rate (U.S. note 30).
inEffect.whatItMeans: Most Russian Chapter 68 goods pay 32.5% to 72.5%; fiber-cement articles 1.7¢–2.2¢/kg plus 12.5%.

inEffect.country: Other Section 301 economies (incl. Israel, Malaysia, Taiwan, the UK, the UAE, Switzerland)
inEffect.now: +10% or 10% (in place of base) or +12.5% or 12.5% (in place of base)
inEffect.exemption: Rates by country: Israel and the UAE +12.5%, Malaysia and the UK +10%, Taiwan 10% and Switzerland 12.5% in total, and the other listed economies +10% or +12.5%. No Chapter 68 line is on the general exemption list (note 52(b)) or any country exception list (note 52(j)). Countries outside the 60 economies pay only the base rate. For quartz surface products, Israel, Korea, Australia, Colombia, Panama, Peru, Singapore, the CAFTA-DR countries, CBERA beneficiaries and the listed developing countries (note 41(c)) pay no safeguard; Malaysia, Taiwan, Thailand and others do.
inEffect.whatItMeans: Israeli engineered quartz pays 12.5% (no safeguard); Malaysian or Taiwanese quartz pays 10% plus the 25%/50% safeguard; UAE asphalt roofing pays the base rate plus 12.5%.

changes.title: No Chapter 68 base-rate changes
changes.detail: All 97 Chapter 68 lines carry the same General, Special and Column 2 rates in 2026 Revision 21 as in the 2025 Basic Edition, and no line was added, split or renumbered.

changes.title: China Section 301 List 3 continues after the four-year review
changes.detail: USTR announced that the 2018 China Section 301 actions did not terminate on their 2026 anniversaries because domestic industries asked for them to continue. For Chapter 68 this keeps +25% (List 3) on every line — stone, quartz, abrasives, mineral wool, gypsum board, friction material and carbon fiber.

changes.title: Canada Section 338 lists revised; Chapter 68 entries kept
changes.detail: Proclamation 11065 modified the provisions on the 9903.03.14 list from September 15, 2026. In Revision 21, which carries the revised list, 6809.11.00 and 6810.99.00 are still listed.

changes.title: Antidumping review of Indian quartz: preliminary results
changes.detail: Commerce published preliminary results of the 2024–2025 administrative review of the antidumping order on quartz surface products from India (A-533-889). Final results will reset the company cash-deposit rates; until then the rates from the last completed review apply.

changes.title: Canada Section 338 duty takes effect on gypsum board and 6810.99 articles
changes.detail: 50% on listed products of Canada after a 3-day suspension lapsed. Chapter 68 is on the motor-vehicle list (9903.03.14) with two subheadings: 6809.11.00 (gypsum board faced with paper — drywall) and 6810.99.00 (other articles of cement, concrete or artificial stone, including quartz slabs). Unlike the Section 301 duty, it applies to USMCA-qualifying goods too (U.S. note 51(a)). Both subheadings remain on the list in Revision 21, after the September 15, 2026 revisions.

changes.title: Section 201 safeguard on quartz surface products takes effect
changes.detail: Proclamation 11051 put a 4-year tariff-rate quota on quartz surface products (6810.99.00.20, 6810.99.00.40 and 7020.00.60): +25% (9903.45.30) within a quota of 13,006,426 m² for the first year, filled quarter by quarter (3,251,606 m² each), and +50% (9903.45.31) over it. The duty stacks on the base rate, the Section 301 duties and the antidumping and countervailing duties. Canada, Mexico, Australia, Colombia, Israel, Korea, Panama, Peru, Singapore, the CAFTA-DR countries, CBERA beneficiaries and listed developing countries (U.S. note 41(c)) are excluded. Granite, marble, soapstone and quartzite are outside the scope.

changes.title: Scheduled: quartz safeguard rates step down each August 15
changes.detail: Under U.S. note 41(d)–(e) the in-quota rate falls to 23% and the over-quota rate to 49% for entries from August 15, 2027 (quota 14,771,583 m²), then 21%/48% from August 15, 2028 (15,236,099 m²) and 19%/47% from August 15, 2029 (15,700,614 m²). The safeguard ends after August 14, 2030.

changes.title: Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies cover all of Chapter 68
changes.detail: 10% or 12.5% on all products of 60 economies (9903.05.20–9903.05.84). No Chapter 68 line is on the general exemption list (note 52(b)) or on any country exception list (note 52(j)); only civil-aircraft articles of 6812–6813 are relieved (note 52(d)). EU goods pay 10% in total and Japanese goods 12.5% in total — every Chapter 68 base rate is below both. India and the UK +10%; Turkey, Vietnam and Brazil +12.5%. USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico are exempt (9903.05.93, 9903.05.94).

changes.title: Section 122 import surcharge expired
changes.detail: The 150-day surcharge (9903.03.01) expired at the close of July 23, 2026.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on products of Brazil; quartzite exempt
changes.detail: 25% on all goods of Brazil (9903.05.01), except the subheadings in U.S. note 50(a)(ii) (9903.05.03). For Chapter 68 that list names one subheading, 6802.99.00 — worked quartzite, sandstone and other stone — so Brazilian quartzite slabs pay no Brazil duty, while granite (6802.93), marble and every other Chapter 68 good pays it. From July 24 the 12.5% forced-labor tariff (9903.05.27) is added on top of both.

changes.title: Diamond saw-blade order: Commerce finds dumping likely to continue
changes.detail: In the third sunset review of the 2009 antidumping order on diamond sawblades and parts from China (A-570-900), Commerce found that revocation would likely lead to dumping at margins up to 164.09%. The order — which reaches diamond segments for circular sawblades entered under 6804.21.00 — stays in force while the USITC completes its expedited review.

changes.title: Magnesia carbon brick orders enter their third five-year review
changes.detail: Commerce and the USITC started sunset reviews of the antidumping orders on magnesia carbon bricks from China and Mexico and the countervailing duty order on China (A-570-954, A-201-837, C-570-955). The scope covers bricks entered under 6815.91 and 6815.99 as well as heading 6902; the orders stay in force during the reviews.

changes.title: USMCA joint review: not renewed, still in force
changes.detail: The United States did not agree to renew the USMCA in its current form. USTR said the Agreement remains in force pending resolution of the issues or until termination, so USMCA claims (SPI S) still remove the base rate and the Section 301 duty on Mexican and Canadian goods — but not the Section 338 duty on Canadian gypsum board and 6810.99 articles.

changes.title: EPA ban on chrysotile asbestos sheet gaskets takes effect
changes.detail: After May 27, 2026 no one may manufacture or import chrysotile asbestos, or articles containing it, for sheet gaskets used in chemical production (40 CFR 751.509(a)); titanium dioxide and nuclear-material users have until May 28, 2029 (Savannah River Site 2037). This reaches compressed asbestos fiber jointing and gaskets of 6812.99.

changes.title: USITC finds serious injury from quartz imports (Section 201)
changes.detail: The USITC sent the President its report in investigation TA-201-79, finding that quartz surface products are imported in such increased quantities as to be a substantial cause of serious injury to the U.S. industry, and recommending relief. USTR took comments and held a hearing in June; the President proclaimed the safeguard on July 31, 2026.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge replaces the IEEPA tariffs
changes.detail: 10% on products of all countries (9903.03.01) until July 23, 2026. No Chapter 68 subheading was on the product exemption list (9903.03.03); civil-aircraft articles of 6812–6813 were relieved (9903.03.05). USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico were exempt.

changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended the Canada, Mexico, China, Brazil, India and reciprocal duties, and CBP stopped collecting them for goods entered from 12:00 a.m. ET on February 24. The 9903.01.xx and 9903.02.xx headings are still printed in Revision 21 but are no longer in effect.

changes.title: India's extra 25% IEEPA duty removed
changes.detail: Executive Order 14384 ended the additional 25% duty on products of India (9903.01.84) from February 7, 2026. The 25% reciprocal rate on India ended with the other IEEPA duties on February 24.

changes.title: Scheduled: Section 301 tariff on products of Nicaragua
changes.detail: Products of Nicaragua that pay the column 1-general rate (that is, not entered under CAFTA-DR) will pay +10% (9903.89.01) from January 1, 2027 and +15% from January 1, 2028. Today Nicaragua pays the 12.5% 2026 Section 301 duty (9903.05.58).

changes.title: Quartz antidumping and countervailing orders on India and Turkey continued
changes.detail: After the first five-year reviews, the USITC found that revoking the orders would likely lead to continued injury, and Commerce continued the antidumping (A-533-889, A-489-837) and countervailing (C-533-890, C-489-838) orders on quartz surface products from India and Turkey, effective December 18, 2025.

changes.title: USITC opens a Section 201 safeguard investigation on quartz
changes.detail: On a petition by U.S. producers, the USITC instituted investigation TA-201-79 into whether increased imports of quartz surface products from all countries cause serious injury — the first step toward the 2026 safeguard tariff.

changes.title: China fentanyl duty cut to 10%
changes.detail: The IEEPA duty on products of China and Hong Kong (9903.01.24) fell from +20% to +10%. It ended with the other IEEPA duties on February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Antidumping and countervailing orders on Chinese sol-gel abrasive grains
changes.detail: Commerce issued orders on sol gel alumina-based ceramic abrasive grains from China (A-570-190, C-570-191): 88.32% antidumping (China-wide) and 165.05% countervailing. The scope covers the grains whether or not incorporated into abrasive papers, grinding wheels and discs — only the grain component, not the whole article — and lists 6804.22 and 6805 subheadings among the classifications.

changes.title: Extra 25% on products of India
changes.detail: Executive Order 14329 added 25% on Indian goods (9903.01.84), on top of the 25% reciprocal rate in force since August 7, 2025 (EO 14326): 50% in all on Indian granite, sandstone and quartz, on top of the base rate and any antidumping duty. Ended February 7, 2026.

changes.title: Country reciprocal rates replace the 10% baseline
changes.detail: Executive Order 14326 set country rates for goods entered from August 7, 2025: India +25%, Vietnam +20%, Turkey +15%, Brazil and the UK +10%. EU goods with a column 1 rate under 15% — every Chapter 68 line — paid 15% in total (9903.02.20). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional 40% on products of Brazil; quartzite exempt
changes.detail: Executive Order 14323 added 40% on Brazilian goods (9903.01.77) on top of the 10% reciprocal duty — 50% in all on Brazilian granite and marble. Its exemption list (9903.01.81) named 6802.99.00, so Brazilian quartzite paid only the 10%. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Canada additional duty raised to 35%
changes.detail: Raised the IEEPA duty on non-USMCA Canadian goods to +35% (9903.01.10). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: China reciprocal duty cut from 125% to 10%
changes.detail: Executive Order 14298 cut the reciprocal duty on Chinese goods to 10% for goods entered from May 14, 2025. A Chinese granite countertop then paid 3.7% + 25% (List 3) + 20% + 10% = 58.7% until November 9, 2025. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: China reciprocal duty raised to 125%
changes.detail: Executive Order 14266 raised the reciprocal duty on Chinese goods to 125% from April 10, 2025, and paused the higher country rates announced on April 2 for other countries, which never took effect. With the 20% fentanyl duty and the 25% List 3 duty, a Chinese granite countertop paid 173.7% until May 13, 2025.

changes.title: Reciprocal tariff on products of all countries
changes.detail: 10% baseline (9903.01.25) from April 5, 2025, and country rates (9903.02.xx); Canada and Mexico excluded. No Chapter 68 product was on the Annex II exemption list. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: China fentanyl duty raised to 20%
changes.detail: The IEEPA duty on products of China and Hong Kong (9903.01.20, then 9903.01.24) went from +10% (from February 4, 2025) to +20%, on top of the List 3 duty. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duty on products of Mexico
changes.detail: +25% on non-USMCA goods (9903.01.01); USMCA-qualifying goods exempt (9903.01.04). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duty on products of Canada
changes.detail: +25% on non-USMCA goods (9903.01.10), later raised to +35%; USMCA-qualifying goods exempt (9903.01.14). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Quartz antidumping and countervailing orders on China continued
changes.detail: After the first sunset reviews Commerce continued the 2019 antidumping (A-570-084) and countervailing (C-570-085) duty orders on quartz surface products from China, effective January 24, 2025.

changes.title: EPA bans imports of chrysotile asbestos brakes, friction products and gaskets
changes.detail: EPA's 2024 TSCA rule prohibits the manufacture (including import), processing and distribution of chrysotile asbestos, and articles containing it, for oilfield brake blocks, aftermarket automotive brakes and linings, other vehicle friction products and other gaskets after November 25, 2024 (40 CFR 751.509(d)–(e)). For Chapter 68 this reaches asbestos friction material of 6813.20 and asbestos gaskets and jointing of 6812.

changes.title: Antidumping and countervailing orders on quartz from India and Turkey
changes.detail: Commerce issued antidumping orders on quartz surface products from India (A-533-889; 0.33%–3.58% cash deposits, all others 1.02%) and Turkey (A-489-837; 5.13%), and countervailing orders (C-533-890; India all others 2.17%; C-489-838; Turkey 2.43%). The rates have since been reset in administrative reviews.

changes.title: Antidumping and countervailing orders on quartz from China
changes.detail: Commerce issued antidumping (A-570-084) and countervailing (C-570-085) duty orders on quartz surface products from China: antidumping cash deposits of 255.27%–295.02% for examined and separate-rate companies and 326.15% for the China-wide entity, and countervailing rates of 45.32% to 190.99%.

changes.title: China List 3 duty raised to 25%
changes.detail: USTR raised the List 3 duty (9903.88.03) from 10% to 25%. List 3 covers every Chapter 68 subheading, and the rate has applied ever since.

changes.title: China Section 301 List 3 reaches all of Chapter 68
changes.detail: The third China Section 301 list put +10% on Chinese stone, quartz, abrasives, mineral wool, plaster and cement articles, asbestos and friction articles, mica and carbon fiber — every Chapter 68 subheading.

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of Chapter 68 goods were **$9.57B in 2025**, 7.6% less than the $10.36B of 2024 and below the $11.21B peak of 2022. Two headings make up more than half: **worked stone (6802)**, $3.09B — marble and travertine $1.24B, quartzite and other stone $819M (up 32.8%), granite $571M (down 21.0%) — and **concrete and artificial-stone articles (6810)**, $2.46B, of which 6810.99 — the line for engineered quartz and other articles — was $2.27B, down 13.8%. Carbon fiber, graphite and other mineral articles (6815) added $1.08B.

Suppliers specialize. **Mexico** ($1.04B) ships gypsum board ($285M), concrete and artificial-stone articles ($228M) and coated abrasives; **Canada** ($1.03B) asphalt roofing ($385M), 6810 articles ($195M) and mineral wool. **Brazil** ($941M, +9.9%) is the largest stone supplier — $835M of heading 6802 — ahead of **Italy** ($637M) and **Turkey** ($443M). Heading 6810, where engineered quartz is classified, comes mainly from **India** ($477M), **Vietnam** ($401M) and **Thailand** ($267M; Thailand's total imports grew from $53.4M in 2020 to $310M). **China** fell 25.2% to $761M, from $1.03B in 2020 — its quartz has been under antidumping duties since 2019. Germany, Japan, Mexico and France lead heading 6815 (carbon fiber, graphite and other mineral articles).

The figures are annual and stop at 2025, before the 2026 tariff changes (the end of the IEEPA duties in February, the Section 301 tariffs from July 24, the quartz safeguard from August 15 and the Canada Section 338 duties from August 22); they do not show what those changes did. Duty-collected figures are not available from an official source yet.

industryAreas.intro:
Chapter 68 base rates are low — Free to 9% — so the extra duty that **depends on where the goods come from** decides the price. Each cell below is the base rate for that product group plus the extra duty for that country, minus any preference — taken from the current tariff schedule.

Since the IEEPA duties ended on February 24, 2026, the extra duty is mainly the **Section 301 tariff on 60 economies** that started July 24, 2026: **+10% for India**, **+12.5% for Turkey, Vietnam and Thailand**, **10% in total for Italy, Spain, Germany and the rest of the EU** and **12.5% in total for Japan and Korea**. **China adds 37.5%** (12.5% plus the 25% List 3 duty) and **Brazil 37.5%** — except on quartzite and other stone of 6802.99.00, which pays only 12.5%. Engineered quartz from most countries adds the **quartz safeguard** (+25% in quota, +50% over quota), so the 6810 cells show three totals. USMCA-qualifying goods from Mexico pay nothing; from Canada they pay nothing except on gypsum board and 6810.99 articles, which owe the **50% Section 338 duty** whatever is claimed.

Ranges like "Free · 11.8%" mean the group has lines with different base rates; select a cell to see which lines carry which rate.
A per-unit rate plus a percentage cannot be added into one number without the shipment’s weight, count or volume, so it is shown as written.

tariffEngineering.h1: HTS Chapter 68: Stone, Quartz, Plaster, Cement & Abrasives — Import Documents & Ways to Lower Duty

seo.title: Importing Quartz Slabs, Granite, Stone & Asbestos Articles into the U.S.: Safeguard, AD/CVD, EPA Rules & Legal Ways to Lower Duty (HTS Ch. 68) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: What each HTS Chapter 68 line needs at U.S. entry — the quartz safeguard headings, antidumping and countervailing deposits on Chinese, Indian and Turkish quartz, EPA asbestos bans and notice rules, country-of-origin marking — and the legal ways to pay less: quartz-versus-natural-stone classification, origin, USMCA and FTAs, the Brazil quartzite exemption, first sale, drawback, FTZ and rulings.

tariffEngineering.intro:
Most Chapter 68 goods need no import license, but three things decide what a shipment costs and whether it may enter at all. **Engineered quartz** (6810.99.00.20/.40) is the most regulated product in the chapter: it pays the 2026 **Section 201 safeguard** (+25% in quota, +50% over quota) unless it comes from an excluded country, and from China, India and Turkey it also carries **antidumping and countervailing duty deposits**. **Asbestos** articles of 6811–6813 fall under EPA's Toxic Substances Control Act rules: chrysotile asbestos for vehicle brakes, friction products and gaskets may no longer be imported, and other asbestos uses need EPA notice first. And every article must be **marked with its country of origin**.

On cost, the base rates are low (Free to 9%), so the levers that matter are the extra duties: what the product is (natural quartzite or granite is outside the quartz safeguard and the quartz trade-remedy orders, and Brazilian quartzite is exempt from the Brazil duty), where it was made, and whether USMCA, an FTA, the civil-aircraft provisions, first-sale valuation, drawback or a foreign-trade zone applies. Each lever depends on a document, listed below with its regulation.

levers.title: Know whether the goods are quartz surface products — or natural stone
levers.saves: The 25%–50% safeguard, and (from China, India or Turkey) the antidumping and countervailing duties, which reach engineered quartz but not natural stone
levers.appliesTo: 6810.99.00.20 and 6810.99.00.40 (agglomerated quartz slabs), and natural stone of heading 6802 that is sold as "quartzite" or "granite"
levers.document: A composition sheet showing the share of silica, resin binder and other materials by weight; for natural stone, the quarry and a petrographic description.
levers.caveat: Under U.S. note 41(a) a surface product is QSP when silica is the largest single material by weight and it is bound with resin — pigments or cement do not take it out, and cutting, polishing or fabricating it in a third country does not change that. Quarried granite, marble, soapstone and quartzite are outside the scope. A name on the invoice decides nothing; the material does.

Entries beyond the quarter's quantity must use the over-quota heading. Goods from excluded countries do not count against the quota.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 41(d)–(e)

levers.title: Know the country of origin
levers.saves: The difference between country rates: no safeguard for quartz from Canada, Mexico, Israel, Korea, Brazil, Indonesia and the other note 41(c) countries; +10% Section 301 for India or the UK, +12.5% for Turkey or Vietnam, 10% in total for the EU, +37.5% for China
levers.appliesTo: All lines; the gap is widest on engineered quartz and on Chinese and Brazilian stone
levers.document: Production records showing where the article was made — for stone, where it was quarried and worked; for quartz, where the slab was cast.
levers.caveat: Cutting, polishing or edging a slab made elsewhere may not move its origin, and for quartz the safeguard and the antidumping and countervailing orders follow the country where the QSP was manufactured, including when it is finished or fabricated in a third country.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 20, 41, 50–52

levers.title: Classify the stone by what it is — quartzite is not granite
levers.saves: From Brazil: 25 points — quartzite and other stone of 6802.99.00 are on the Brazil exemption list (19% in total for a quartzite slab), granite of 6802.93 is not (41.2%). Elsewhere, the base-rate gap between granite (3.7%), marble (2.5%–4.9%) and other stone (6.5%)
levers.appliesTo: Heading 6802 — slabs, tiles, countertops and monuments of natural stone
levers.document: A petrographic or mineralogical description of the stone; for slabs, thickness and edge work (additional U.S. note 1).
levers.caveat: Commercial names ("granite" for many quartzites and gneisses, "marble" for some limestones) do not decide the line. Chapter 68 note 2 puts quartzite in heading 6802 as "other" stone, and the exemption is by subheading — the goods must actually be 6802.99 stone. A ruling settles doubtful cases.

citations.label: HTSUS Chapter 68 notes and additional U.S. notes
HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 50(a)(ii), 9903.05.03

levers.title: Claim USMCA on goods from Mexico or Canada
levers.saves: The base rate (up to 9%) plus the 10% Section 301 duty
levers.appliesTo: All lines from Mexico; from Canada, every line except 6809.11.00 (gypsum board) and 6810.99.00, which owe the 50% Section 338 duty even under USMCA
levers.document: A certification of origin from the importer, exporter or producer, kept ready for CBP.
levers.caveat: USMCA does not remove the 50% Section 338 duty on the Canadian subheadings in U.S. note 51(b)(3). The good must meet the Chapter 68 rule of origin in General Note 11 for its subheading. The USMCA was not renewed at the July 1, 2026 joint review but remains in force.

citations.label: HTSUS General Note 11 (USMCA rules of origin)

levers.title: Claim an FTA, AGOA or CAFTA-DR rate
levers.saves: The base rate on dutiable lines; for quartz, FTA partners on the note 41(c) list (Australia, Colombia, Israel, Korea, Panama, Peru, Singapore, the CAFTA-DR countries) also pay no safeguard
levers.appliesTo: Dutiable lines whose Special column lists the program: AU, BH, CL, CO, D (AGOA), E (CBERA), IL, JO, KR, MA, OM, P (CAFTA-DR), PA, PE, SG
levers.document: The origin proof each program requires and records to back it up.
levers.caveat: An FTA removes the base rate but not the 2026 Section 301 duty (U.S. note 52(a)). The safeguard exclusion in note 41(c) goes by country of origin, not by whether a preference is claimed. GSP (A, A*) has been expired since December 31, 2020; AGOA (D) runs to December 31, 2026.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 41(c), 52(a)

levers.title: Use the China List 3 exclusion for qualifying sandstone pavers
levers.saves: The 25% List 3 duty on Chinese sandstone that matches the exclusion description
levers.appliesTo: 6802.99.00.90 — "brown wave" sandstone with one textured side and up to four chiseled edges (density 2,750 kg/m³), and flamed-finish sandstone 200–3,100 mm long, 100–1,380 mm wide and 30–180 mm thick
levers.document: Product specifications showing the stone matches the description; report 9903.88.69 instead of 9903.88.03.
levers.caveat: In effect through November 9, 2026 unless USTR extends it again. The 12.5% 2026 Section 301 duty (9903.05.31) still applies.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 20(vvv)(iii), 9903.88.69

levers.title: Claim civil-aircraft treatment for aircraft friction and asbestos parts
levers.saves: The 2026 Section 301 duty (note 52(d), 9903.05.88) and, for Canada, the Section 338 duty (9903.03.16)
levers.appliesTo: 6812.80.90, 6812.99, 6813.20, 6813.81 and 6813.89 articles for use in civil aircraft that meet general note 6
levers.document: The civil-aircraft certification CBP requires for "Free (C)" treatment, and records of the aircraft use.
levers.caveat: Only articles for civil aircraft qualify; military and (for Canada) unmanned aircraft are out. Asbestos-containing articles remain subject to EPA's rules.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 51(d), 52(d)

levers.title: Value at the first sale for export when you buy through a middleman
levers.saves: Every ad valorem duty is charged on a lower value — the base rate, the 10%–37.5% Section 301 duties and the 25%–50% safeguard included — when the factory price to a trading company is lower than the price you pay
levers.appliesTo: All lines bought through a trading company, distributor or agent-buyer rather than straight from the quarry or plant
levers.document: Proof that the first sale was a bona fide sale for export to the United States at arm's length: the factory invoice, contracts and payment records.
levers.caveat: Only a sale clearly destined for the U.S. qualifies. Antidumping and countervailing duties are assessed under Commerce's own rules, not lowered this way.

levers.title: Recover duty on goods you export or destroy
levers.saves: Up to 99% of the duties paid, when the imported goods (or goods made from them) are exported or destroyed
levers.appliesTo: Any line — for example slabs cut into countertops for export, or abrasives used to make exported goods
levers.document: A drawback claim to CBP with import, manufacturing and export records.
levers.caveat: Antidumping and countervailing duties are not refundable as drawback. Claims have filing deadlines and record-keeping rules; check whether a given Chapter 99 duty is eligible before relying on it.

levers.title: Hold or process goods in a foreign-trade zone
levers.saves: No duty on goods re-exported from the zone, and duty deferred until goods leave it for the U.S. market
levers.appliesTo: Any line — useful for stone and quartz distributed to several countries
levers.document: Zone admission (CBP Form 214) and the zone operator's inventory records.
levers.caveat: Quartz surface products admitted on or after August 15, 2026 must be in privileged foreign status (19 CFR 146.41), so they pay the safeguard rate of their classification when entered for consumption. Goods entered from a zone pay the duties in force on the entry date.

levers.title: Use a Chapter 98 provision for U.S. goods coming back
levers.saves: All duty on U.S.-made goods returned unchanged (9801.00.10)
levers.appliesTo: Any line, for American goods returned without having been advanced in value or improved abroad
levers.document: Proof of U.S. origin and of the export, as CBP requires for the provision.
levers.caveat: The Section 301 and 338 duties also do not apply to goods properly entered under Chapter 98, except subchapter XXIII and 9802.00.40–9802.00.80 (U.S. notes 51(a) and 52(a)).

levers.title: Get a binding classification ruling
levers.saves: Certainty where the line decides the rate and the extra duty: engineered quartz (6810.99) versus natural quartzite (6802.99) or granite (6802.93); a slab versus a tile; mounted versus unmounted brake linings (6813 or 8708.30)
levers.appliesTo: Any line where the material, thickness or use decides the line
levers.document: A ruling request to CBP describing the article, its composition, dimensions and use.
levers.caveat: Rulings apply to the transaction described; a CBP ruling does not decide whether goods are within an antidumping order's scope — Commerce does.

rules.title: Quartz surface products: report 9903.45.30 (in quota, +25%) or 9903.45.31 (over quota, +50%) with the line unless the goods are a product of a note 41(c) country; QSP admitted to a foreign-trade zone must be in privileged foreign status

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 41

rules.title: Quartz surface products from China, India or Turkey are subject merchandise under antidumping and countervailing duty orders: enter them as AD/CVD entries with the case numbers and cash deposits (A-570-084, C-570-085; A-533-889, C-533-890; A-489-837, C-489-838), and file the importer's non-reimbursement certificate. The written scope, not the HTS line, decides coverage

Other orders that reach Chapter 68 lines: diamond saw-blade segments from China (A-570-900, 6804.21.00); sol gel alumina-based abrasive grains from China, including the grain component of wheels and coated abrasives (A-570-190, C-570-191, 6804.22 and 6805); magnesia carbon bricks from China and Mexico (A-570-954, C-570-955, A-201-837, 6815.91 and 6815.99)

Chrysotile asbestos, and articles containing it, may not be imported for aftermarket automotive brakes and linings, other vehicle friction products, oilfield brake blocks or other gaskets (since November 25, 2024), or for sheet gaskets used in chemical production (since May 27, 2026, with limited exceptions to 2029)

Any other import of asbestos — including as part of an article, such as asbestos-cement products, millboard, packings, woven products or other friction materials — is a significant new use that needs a notice to EPA at least 90 days before import. Flooring felt, rollboard and commercial, corrugated and specialty paper containing asbestos remain banned
Importers of substances regulated under TSCA section 6, chrysotile asbestos included, are subject to the TSCA import certification rules

Country-of-origin marking in English, legible, indelible and permanent enough to reach the ultimate purchaser — on the article or, where the article cannot be marked, its container. Mica not further manufactured than cut or stamped to shape is on the exception list (its container must be marked)

Report the Chapter 99 headings with the line: the 2026 Section 301 heading for the country, China List 3 (9903.88.03) or its exclusion (9903.88.69), Brazil (9903.05.01) or its exemption (9903.05.03), Canada Section 338 (9903.03.14), Russia (9903.90.08)

groups.label: Setts, curbstones & flagstones of natural stone
groups.note: No agency license. Rough blocks and unworked stone are in Chapter 25.

groups.label: Worked stone: granite, marble, travertine, quartzite & other monumental or building stone
groups.note: No agency license. Natural stone — granite, marble, quartzite — is outside the quartz safeguard and the quartz antidumping orders. Brazilian 6802.99.00 stone (quartzite) is exempt from the 25% Brazil duty; Chinese sandstone pavers of 6802.99.00.90 may use the List 3 exclusion.

groups.label: Worked slate & slate articles (incl. roofing slate)
groups.note: No agency license. Roofing slate pays 3.3%, other slate is Free.

groups.label: Millstones, grindstones & grinding wheels (incl. diamond and resin-bonded)
groups.note: Diamond segments for circular sawblades (6804.21.00.10) from China are covered by the 2009 antidumping order; wheels made with Chinese sol-gel alumina grains carry the 2025 orders on the grain component.

groups.label: Coated abrasives: sandpaper, abrasive cloth, belts & discs
groups.note: Sandpaper, belts and discs made with Chinese sol-gel alumina abrasive grains carry the 2025 antidumping and countervailing duties on the grain component.

groups.label: Mineral wool (rock & slag wool), vermiculite & expanded clays
groups.note: No agency license for mineral wool, vermiculite or calcium silicate.

groups.label: Asphalt articles: roofing rolls, shingles & siding
groups.note: No agency license. Asphalt rolls are Free, shingles and siding 2.7%.

groups.label: Wood-wool, straw & fiber panels bonded with cement or plaster
Plaster articles: gypsum board (drywall), plaster panels & tiles
groups.note: Paper-faced gypsum board (6809.11.00) from Canada pays the 50% Section 338 duty even under USMCA.

groups.label: Cement, concrete & artificial stone: engineered quartz slabs, tiles, blocks & precast
groups.note: Engineered quartz (6810.99.00.20/.40) pays the safeguard and, from China, India and Turkey, antidumping and countervailing duties; the orders' written scope also reaches quartz entered under other 6810 lines. 6810.99.00 from Canada pays the 50% Section 338 duty even under USMCA.

groups.label: Fiber-cement (asbestos-cement and cellulose fiber-cement) sheets, panels & pipes
groups.note: Asbestos-cement articles (6811.40) need an EPA significant new use notice before import; cellulose fiber-cement is unrestricted.

groups.note: Asbestos articles: gaskets and friction uses of chrysotile asbestos are banned from import; other uses need EPA notice first. Asbestos footwear pays 8.3%.

groups.note: No agency license. Mica cut or stamped to shape may be marked on its container.

finalConclusion.intro: Straight answers to the most common questions about U.S. tariffs and import rules for quartz, granite, marble and other Chapter 68 goods. Each answer links to the page with the full detail.
keyTakeaways: 42 of the 97 Chapter 68 lines carry a base duty, all of it low: granite 3.7%, marble slabs 2.5%, quartzite and other stone 6.5%, mineral wool 3.9%, concrete tiles up to 9%. Engineered quartz slabs, sandpaper, gypsum board and carbon fiber are Free.

Since August 15, 2026 engineered quartz (6810.99.00.20/.40) pays a Section 201 safeguard: +25% within the quarterly quota, +50% over it, stepping down each August to 2030. Canada, Mexico, Brazil, Israel, Korea, the CAFTA-DR countries and listed developing countries are excluded.

Since July 24, 2026 a Section 301 duty is added by country: +10% India, +12.5% Turkey, Vietnam and Thailand, 10% in total for the EU, 12.5% in total for Japan and Korea. China pays +37.5% on every line; Brazil +37.5% except quartzite and other stone of 6802.99.00 (+12.5%).

Quartz from China, India and Turkey also carries antidumping and countervailing duties, continued in 2025; diamond saw-blade segments, sol-gel abrasive grains and magnesia carbon bricks from China (and bricks from Mexico) have their own orders.
USMCA-qualifying goods from Mexico pay nothing; Canadian gypsum board and 6810.99 articles pay 50% Section 338 even under USMCA.

The IEEPA duties ended February 24, 2026 and the 10% Section 122 surcharge July 23, 2026. EPA bans the import of chrysotile asbestos brakes, friction products and gaskets; other asbestos articles need EPA notice first.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on quartz countertops?
faqs.answer: Yes. Engineered quartz slabs and countertops (6810.99.00.20/.40) are Free in the base column, but since August 15, 2026 they pay a Section 201 safeguard (Proclamation 11051): +25% while the quarterly quota of 3,251,606 m² is open (9903.45.30) and +50% once it is filled (9903.45.31), falling to 23%/49% on August 15, 2027 and ending August 14, 2030. The Section 301 duty for the country is added: Vietnamese or Thai quartz pays 37.5% or 62.5%, Indian 35% or 60%, Spanish or Italian 35% or 60%, Chinese 62.5% or 87.5%. Quartz from Canada, Mexico, Brazil, Israel, Korea, Indonesia and other countries on the note 41(c) list pays no safeguard.

faqs.question: Is there an antidumping duty on quartz from India, China or Turkey?
searchedAs: anti dumping duty on quartz from india
faqs.answer: Yes. Commerce antidumping and countervailing duty orders cover quartz surface products from China (since 2019: A-570-084, C-570-085, continued January 2025) and from India (A-533-889, C-533-890) and Turkey (A-489-837, C-489-838), both since 2020 and continued in December 2025. At the orders, China-wide cash deposits were 326.15% antidumping plus 45.32% or more countervailing; India 0.33%–3.58% antidumping plus about 2% countervailing; Turkey 5.13% plus 2.43%. Commerce resets company rates in annual reviews. These duties are on top of the safeguard and the Section 301 duty.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on quartzite from Brazil?
searchedAs: tariffs on quartzite from brazil to usa
faqs.answer: Quartzite slabs (6802.99.00.50) have a 6.5% base rate. Brazil pays the 12.5% Section 301 duty (9903.05.27), but 6802.99.00 is on the exemption list of the 25% Brazil Section 301 duty (U.S. note 50(a)(ii)), so a quartzite slab pays 19% in total. Natural quartzite is not a quartz surface product, so the quartz safeguard does not apply. Brazil supplied $835M of worked stone in 2025.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on granite from India, China and Brazil?
searchedAs: is there a tariff on granite
faqs.answer: Granite slabs, countertops and monuments (6802.93) have a 3.7% base rate. Indian granite pays 13.7% (+10% Section 301), Brazilian 41.2% (+12.5% and the 25% Brazil duty — granite is not on its exemption list), Chinese 41.2% (+12.5% and 25% List 3), Italian or Spanish 10% in total, Turkish or Vietnamese 16.2%. USMCA-qualifying Mexican or Canadian granite pays nothing. Granite is natural stone, so the quartz safeguard does not apply.

faqs.question: What are the tariffs on marble from Italy and Turkey?
faqs.answer: Marble slabs pay 2.5% (6802.91.05), other worked marble 4.9% and marble simply cut or sawn 1.9%. Italian (or other EU) marble pays 10% in total since July 24, 2026 (9903.05.39) — $1,000 on $10,000 of slabs — instead of 15% in late 2025. Turkish marble pays the base rate plus 12.5%: 15% for slabs. Italy supplied $637M and Turkey $443M of worked stone in 2025.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on natural stone and stone countertops?
faqs.answer: Yes, but natural stone pays far less than engineered quartz. Base rates run from 1.9% to 6.5% (heading 6802), and the 2026 Section 301 duty is added by country: 10% in total from the EU, +10% from India, +12.5% from Turkey or Vietnam, +37.5% from China and from Brazil (except quartzite and other 6802.99 stone, +12.5%). Granite, marble, soapstone and quartzite are outside the quartz safeguard and the quartz antidumping orders.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for quartz slabs and quartz countertops?
searchedAs: hs code for quartz stone slabs
faqs.answer: Engineered (agglomerated) quartz slabs of the type used for countertops are 6810.99.00: 6810.99.00.20 for rectangular slabs at least 3 m long and 1.25 m wide, 6810.99.00.40 for other quartz slabs and countertops. Quartz tiles may fall in 6810.19.12. Natural quartzite is worked stone of 6802.99.00 (slabs 6802.99.00.50). Quartz sand and crystals are in Chapters 25 and 71.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for granite slabs, countertops and tiles?
faqs.answer: Polished or further-worked granite is 6802.93.00 (3.7%): 6802.93.00.10 for building pieces not cut to size, 6802.93.00.20/.25 for pieces cut to size up to 1.5 cm or 7.5 cm thick (slabs, tiles, countertops), 6802.93.00.35 for monuments. Granite simply cut or sawn with a flat surface is 6802.23.00 (3.7%); small tiles under 7 cm are 6802.10.00 (4.8%). Rough granite blocks are 2516.11 or 2516.12 (Chapter 25).

faqs.question: What is the HS code for marble slabs and tiles?
searchedAs: hs code for marble table top
faqs.answer: Marble slabs (flat pieces up to 5.1 cm thick, additional U.S. note 1) are 6802.91.05.00 (2.5%); other worked marble, including tiles whose face is 7 cm or more across, is 6802.91.15.00 (4.9%); marble simply cut or sawn is 6802.21.50.00 (1.9%). Marble blocks are heading 2515 (Chapter 25), and marble statues that are works of art are Chapter 97.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for grinding wheels and sandpaper?
searchedAs: hs code for diamond grinding wheel
faqs.answer: Grinding wheels and discs without frameworks are heading 6804: diamond wheels 6804.21.00 (Free), wheels bonded with synthetic resin 6804.22.10 (5¢/kg + 2%), vitrified abrasive wheels 6804.22.40 (Free). Sandpaper is 6805.20.00 (on paper), abrasive cloth 6805.10.00 and belts and discs on other backings 6805.30 — all Free. Chinese diamond saw-blade segments and products made with Chinese sol-gel alumina grains carry antidumping duties.

faqs.question: What are the HS codes for gypsum board, mineral wool and cement board?
searchedAs: hs code for rock wool board
hs code for fiber cement board
faqs.answer: Paper-faced gypsum board (drywall) is 6809.11.00 (Free; 6809.11.00.10 for gypsum plaster); other plaster boards 6809.19.00 (3%). Rock and slag wool batts, boards and pipe coverings are 6806.10.00 (3.9%). Fiber-cement board and siding without asbestos is 6811.82.00 (Free); cement backer board of other concrete is 6810.99.00.80. Canadian gypsum board pays the 50% Section 338 duty even under USMCA.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for carbon fiber?
searchedAs: hs code for carbon fiber fabric
hs code for carbon fiber sheet
faqs.answer: Carbon fibers are 6815.11.00, fabrics of carbon fibers 6815.12.00 and other articles of carbon fibers for non-electrical uses 6815.13.00 — all Free in the base column. The Section 301 duty applies by country: 10% in total from the EU, 12.5% in total from Japan or Korea, +37.5% from China. Parts made for a specific machine or vehicle are usually classified with that article.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for brake linings and brake pads?
faqs.answer: Friction material that is not mounted — brake lining in rolls or segments, unmounted pads, clutch facings — is heading 6813: 6813.81.00 for brake linings and pads without asbestos, 6813.89.00 for other friction material, 6813.20.00 if it contains asbestos — all Free. Brake pads and shoes mounted for motor vehicles are 8708.30. Asbestos friction products for vehicles may not be imported under EPA's 2024 rule.

faqs.question: Is asbestos banned in the U.S.? Can asbestos products be imported?
searchedAs: is asbestos banned in the us
is asbestos illegal in the us
is asbestos completely banned in the us
are asbestos products banned in the us
faqs.answer: Partly. EPA's 2024 TSCA rule bans importing chrysotile asbestos, or articles containing it, for aftermarket automotive brakes and linings, other vehicle friction products, oilfield brake blocks and other gaskets (since November 25, 2024) and for sheet gaskets in chemical production (since May 27, 2026, with limited exceptions to 2029). Flooring felt and asbestos paper products have been banned since the 1990s, and any other asbestos use — asbestos-cement products, millboard, packings — needs a significant new use notice to EPA 90 days before import. Asbestos articles are classified in 6811.40, 6812 and 6813.20.
